# Trellis Consumer Guide

Operation starts default to canonical routing. Persist deployment, invocation
ULID, and frozen input before an explicit targeted start. TypeScript uses
`.start(undefined, { invocationId, targetDeploymentId })`; Rust generated invokers
use `start_on_deployment_with_invocation_id(deployment_id, invocation_id, &input)`.
Cancellation-first adds `cancellationRequested: true` in TypeScript or uses
`start_cancelled_on_deployment_with_invocation_id` in Rust, requiring Invoke and
Cancel. Targets never fall back, and choosing a target after losing a canonical
reply does not recover its unknown owner. Deduplication stays deployment-scoped;
accepted references and controls, including replica takeover, are unchanged.

Rust and Node replicas use one deployment-scoped Operation storage codec. This
pre-release persistence cutover does not migrate earlier records: retain existing
installations unchanged and use fresh development/test state. Unsupported records
fail visibly; the runtime never deletes or recreates them as empty state.

Distinct-user live tests use ordinary accounts and explicit grants. Node exposes
`createUser`, `grantUserCapabilities`, and `registerClient`/`connectClient` with
`user`. Rust exposes `create_user`, `grant_user_capabilities`,
`register_native_application`, and `login_native_application_as` (or
`register_client_as`). One app registration supports independent real OAuth
logins for multiple users. User handles are runtime-owned and expose no password;
explicit-user login never grants or restores revoked capabilities. Existing
seeded-administrator convenience and service-seed provisioning remain unchanged.

Console and the isolated OAuth listener require HTTPS outside explicit loopback
development. The HTTP insecure-origin allowlist does not relax that requirement.

Fresh startup creates the protected administrator and accepted built-in authority
before provider admission. Username defaults to `admin`. Without an initial
password, it emits `adminAccountUrl`, a one-time password-setup link on the isolated
OAuth origin; no default password exists. The link expires after five minutes.
Startup flags `--admin-username`, `--admin-password`, and `--admin-password-stdin`
configure fresh credentials. Explicit initialization uses `trellis init admin
--config <path>` with `--username` (default `admin`), optional `--password`, or
`--password-stdin`. Until password setup, each startup prints a fresh setup link
before provider admission and invalidates prior links. After setup, restarts
preserve credentials and emit no replacement link.
Explicit `--reset-admin` supersedes pending links without restoring or recreating
authority. Reset completion revokes existing logins. Ordinary RPCs cannot reset
the protected administrator.

Service Jobs reconstruct retained lifecycle history through the deployment-scoped
runtime `Jobs.History` route automatically. Use generated service job handles;
ordinary service identities cannot read the shared JOBS stream directly. History
pages retain original stream sequences and a fixed upper watermark. The runtime
derives ownership from verified service authority and its current queue binding;
users and other deployments cannot read another deployment's private job history.
Detaching resources retains data. Explicit administrative deletion removes only
the selected detached allocation; shared streams and other queues remain intact.
Recreated job queues have fresh allocation-scoped delivery subjects, while saved
purge cutoffs protect new keyed coordination from delayed old deletions.

Operator CLI: `trellis clients list|get|put|disable|delete` manages public OAuth
registrations, including exact loopback browser redirects.
Auth client flows are fixed on every Put: browser callbacks enable Authorization
Code + refresh; native without callbacks enables Device Code + refresh; native
with callbacks enables both + refresh. Adding/removing native callbacks updates
the supported flows. Kind is immutable; use a new client ID to switch kind.
Native HTTP loopback callbacks need no development flag; browser loopback does.
`put` reads generated AuthOAuthClientPutRequest JSON; mutations are revision-fenced. `trellis apis
list|get|review|accept|force-replace` uses generated Auth request JSON and reviewed
package evidence. Force replacement requires apis.forceReplace and explicit
breakage/consent acknowledgements. Console exposes OAuth clients and API catalog.

Durable event consumers verify original broker publication time. DLQ/replay retains
that provenance in the existing journal and resolves original bytes and timestamp
through authenticated, resource-scoped Events inspection, including after source
expiry. Publisher headers and replay publication time never replace it.

The `accountRead` capability covers account resolution, reading your current
session and signing out of the current login and its application sessions.
`Sessions.Me` and `Sessions.Logout` require normal selection and consent.

Rejected cross-user Device Code reauthorization preserves existing credentials.
Already-open browser tabs refresh discovery from retained trust before spending
refresh tokens. Native renewal uses the current maintenance attachment through
verified authority promotion, including after transport replacement.

Operations use the canonical `<API identity>@v<major>:operation:<action>` identity
across SDKs, storage and complete references; generated aliases are not durable
identities. Canonical starts honor that API major, while owner-directed controls
retain the fixed `operation.v1` transport family. Implementation-only providers
can forward their own updates without receiving caller Observe authority.
Rust generated `OperationRef::reference()` exposes the complete serializable
reference for restoring control without starting another execution.

OIDC claim refresh is scoped to the selected provider and upstream subject; a
second linked identity cannot add or remove another identity's mapped roles.
Direct grants remain independent of upstream role loss and claim freshness.

Configured implied consent applies only to registered browser bindings and their
bounded capability subset. Native and Device Code clients require explicit user
approval even when registered; Device Code confirmation remains mandatory.

Identity-link approval remains a protected same-origin POST. Its no-store
continuation page shows a navigation link to a 60-second, one-use GET handoff
bound to the exact portal session, provider and account. Top-level navigation
reaches the verified IdP without relaxing form-action 'self' or leaking the
handoff in referrers. Direct, expired and replayed handoffs fail.

Cold OAuth resume verifies signed issuer successors from the retained pin using
GET /.well-known/trellis/issuer-chain at the selected OAuth origin and persists
successor trust before spending a refresh token. Unavailable or invalid chains
leave it unspent. A successfully returned new token survives later issuer
verification failure, but its admission remains unusable until authenticated.
Never retry an ambiguously spent predecessor.
Node-native and browser transport recovery reuse admission only while shared verification
accepts its lifetime and current pinned trust. Transport loss alone does not
spend refresh custody. Renewal checks the selected HTTP origin before spending
the token; an ambiguous token POST still requires explicit recovery. Preparation
retries never retransmit application requests or clear known revocations.

Native providers finish accepted RPCs across ordinary authority promotion by
reacquiring a coherent current signing snapshot within one configured deadline.
Handlers are not redispatched; provider, issuer, expiry and revocation checks remain mandatory.
Accepted finite responses may outlive the opening caller context, but not their
request deadline. Current provider verification, known revocation, cancellation
and logical shutdown remain enforced; expired evidence cannot start new work.

Generated Rust Event subscriptions verify original bytes and proof before decoding.
Core NATS requires live publisher authority; durable delivery uses trusted original
publication time, not today's publisher-context expiry. Consumer authority remains current.
If no safe native carrier survives, fresh admission may replace a missed retired
logical session under the same valid provisioned credential and pinned trust.
Removed permissions are not restored, and revoked roots or shutdown cannot recover.
Store object deletion and replacement clean up chunks only in the admitted
identity's allocated Object Store streams, including Operation staging. This
does not authorize KV purge, stream destruction, or cross-owner Store access.

Provisioned services/devices automatically publish the native Health.Heartbeat
event using ordinary SessionEvent signatures. Auth assigns only the runtime-owned
trellis.health@v1::selfReport capability through native provisioning; users/apps
cannot acquire this right. The collector verifies whole catalog authority,
broker chronology, retirement cutoff and signed deployment/instance identity.
The signed trellis.nativeParticipant.v1 extension supplies installed revision and
participant digest, never payload claims. No health declaration is needed in
service contracts. Initial publication is asynchronous, not a connection gate.

Fresh administrator initialization explicitly grants only current accepted
Trellis-owned Auth/Core/State/Health/Jobs/Events capabilities. These grants,
finite platform privileges, and Console/CLI registration commit atomically.
Replay neither grants future capabilities nor rewrites clients. Domain API
access remains explicitly granted; app authority still requires selection,
consent, and client privilege eligibility. `Issuers.Rotate` requires
`privileges.manage`, the expected current key ID, and an idempotency key. Auth
locally generates and durably flushes a private successor key before atomically
committing its old-key-signed chain link, activation, publication intent, and
replay result. Replays do not rotate again. Restart loads the database-current
key and fails closed on missing custody, without replacing the bootstrap seed.
Back up the issuer seed and the database's sibling `<database-stem>.issuer-keys`
directory (`platform.issuer-keys` by default) with Auth's database
and the independent OAuth storage key. Private keys never cross the RPC.
OAuth sessions retain
their original verified refresh family; CONNECT, Authority.Renew, OwnContextGet,
and Admission.Renew consult that exact family's revocation and absolute deadline.
A different live family of the same grant cannot replace it, and rotation never
extends it. Admission.Renew uses the live caller's session-key proof and own
context digest to return same-key signed OAuth admission, at most 300 seconds
and bounded by the candidate authority/family, without rotating refresh tokens.
Invalid roots retire the session and enqueue cutoff/kicks. Provisioned admission
still needs the client's identity signature (`provisioned_signature_required`).

For services, apps, agents, and devices consuming Trellis. Read the
[TypeScript](llms-typescript.txt), [Rust](llms-rust.txt), or
[Svelte](llms-svelte.txt) guide for language-specific usage. Use the guide from
the same release or checkout as the CLI and libraries.

## What Trellis Owns

Own-context bootstrap signs the exact physical socket's broker `attachmentId`
and verifies its echoed signed registry ID; overlapping sockets never select
the newest attachment as a fallback.

Public verification metadata uses the dedicated `trellis.auth.metadata.get`
bootstrap for already admitted connections without an admin capability. Existing
IssuerMetadataRequest/SignedIssuerMetadata messages resolve only requested
authority material, logical status/cutoff, or pinned issuer rotation chains.
Clients verify signatures, retained nonce/subject/reply/scope and freshness using
pinned trust; Missing/Unavailable never clears revocation or grants authority.
Administrative Authority.Status remains a separate protected typed RPC.

Revision 7 Auth unions valid entitlements and intersects them with declared
selection and approved consent in one authoritative transaction. Signed logical
session authority is immutable; reduction retires every live digest under that
session ID. Compatible catalog expansion requires renewal, and cannot silently
approve declined capabilities. Signed revocations remain effective through mirror
reconnect or missing entries until context acceptance deadlines expire.
OAuth/Callout admission and client/provider transports use this authority model;
the old GrantBinding/browser-bind model is not a compatibility option.

OAuth login and consent belong to a separate required portal app and origin
from Console, not a Console route. A different hostname is recommended, not
mandatory: same-hostname origins produce a prominent cookie-scope warning.
Outside explicit loopback development, OAuth and broker transports require
TLS. Keep the provisioned installation identity and independent OAuth storage
key across restarts and issuer rotation. Browser custody uses nonextractable
keys and cross-tab refresh ownership; native custody uses owner-only files and
a cross-process family lock. Dex is an upstream OIDC integration-test
dependency only, never a required Trellis deployment component.

Provisioned native connections receive explicit broker endpoints and pinned
runtime trust from initialization or authenticated provisioning. CONNECT proves
credential possession without asserting a deployment or API. Rust native
applications supply a verified OAuth session to the SDK, which retains custody
and renews admission using the same runtime identity/key and authenticated issuer
pin. Credential-recovery failure closes transport without erasing the durable
record.

Node native applications import `@oatscenter/trellis/native`, discover the selected
issuer, and open `NativeOAuthClient` with explicit scope and trust. The default
custody is process-local memory, with no files or SQLite dependency. Retain an
explicit `MemoryNativeOAuthCustody` object for reconnects within one process.
Remembered login across process restarts requires an application-owned
`NativeOAuthCustody` provider; Trellis ships no persistent Node backend.
Resume explicitly retained credentials or start Device Code with
the generated native request, then connect through `connectNativeClient`.
Persistent providers must exclusively acquire the exact family, durably mark a
refresh token spent before returning it for submission, and atomically retain
successors and authenticated trust. The SDK awaits those commits. A successful
connection owns custody until it closes;
closing an earlier session reference cannot release that ownership. Await native
connection.close() before reacquiring: it joins settled exchanges and asynchronous
lease release, reports release failures, and releases once across repeated closes. Discovery
cannot repin existing credentials; trust advances only through authenticated
issuer rotation. Browser applications retain IndexedDB and Web Locks.
TypeScript signed reply verification waits for already-received ordered revocation
updates before its live checks, without retransmitting requests or bypassing lost
coverage.
Live authority requires an applied initial revocation snapshot and continuing
coverage. Epoch fencing prevents old watchers from changing successor coverage.
TypeScript optional-action checks distinguish missing live authority from denial.
Requests wait for verified authority before publication within their original
deadline and cancellation signal, without replaying requests or bypassing denial.
Rust and TypeScript stage a rollover mirror without withdrawing healthy predecessor
coverage. On mirror failure, one cancellable private supervisor retries snapshot
replay on the surviving attachment while application IO remains fenced; it neither
clears known revocations nor retransmits application requests.
If TypeScript authority expires during coverage loss, private admission obtains
and verifies fresh authority on the surviving attachment before application use
resumes. Snapshot recovery alone never extends expired authority.

Explicit one-off consent overrides older remembered choices without changing
them. Reused choices retain their expiry; later shared withdrawals still retire
affected sessions. A shortened effective authorization deadline is a reduction
unless another entitlement path preserves the outstanding authority.
Consent approval binds the current server-owned presentation and the selected
optional capabilities; stale forms require a fresh presentation. Signed session
authority has a shared 64 KiB issuer, verification, and parsing budget.
Explicitly initialized or administrator-registered development clients may be
eligible for platform privileges. Registration requires clients.manage;
configuring privilege eligibility also requires privileges.manage. Delegation
requires the authenticated user to hold and explicitly approve each privilege.

Finite administrative privilege requests belong to OAuth configuration, not
native IDL or generated application metadata. Browser apps supply
`auth.platformPrivileges: { required, optional }` to their connection. Selecting
an administrative API capability alone grants no finite privilege, and optional
requests remain subject to registration eligibility, user authority, and consent.
Localhost/development mode establishes no trust, and CIMD clients remain
ineligible. Application and OAuth origins remain isolated.

Provisional CIMD client intake shares a 128-client/16 MiB budget and a five-minute
lifetime; live decisions and approved refresh lifecycles are retained. Exhaustion
returns `temporarily_unavailable`, not administrative registration or authority.
Deadlines on newly gained rights bound new contexts, not older narrower contexts
or the logical-session root.

Revision 7's breaking routing cutover uses canonical generated API/action
subjects for RPC, Operation starts, and Live openings. Providers sharing a
logical API share request queues and must be suitable alternatives; identical
IDL does not make independent databases or physical devices interchangeable.
Signed provider identity, generation/action checks, and service-owned resources
remain separate from caller capabilities. Established Live/Transfer traffic
and existing Operation controls retain owner-directed routing. There is no
persisted caller-to-deployment selection or automatic retry of potentially
executed requests. This decision is still being integrated on this branch.

Complete serialized Operation references require `deploymentId`, verified against
certified signed acceptance. SDKs route get/watch/wait/cancel/signals to that
deployment and restore only complete references, never IDs alone. Replicas in
that deployment retain existing executor leases and CAS fencing. The reference
is routing metadata, not authority. Invocation deduplication is deployment-scoped;
an uncertain canonical start must not automatically retry into another deployment.
No cross-deployment idempotency is promised.

Provisioned services/devices prove possession of their identity key and a fresh
runtime/session key for the configured installation/account. Auth derives their
deployment, instance, participant, and implementation authority from current
provisioning records; clients never assert those bindings during CONNECT.
Provisioning still supplies broker endpoints and pinned installation/issuer trust.
Immediate ServiceInstances.Provision and Devices.Provision require identityPublicKey
from a client-owned Ed25519 key. Trellis never stores or returns its private seed.
Missing identityPublicKey returns identity_public_key_required without provisioning
or consuming the idempotency key. provisioningSecret is null; activation-token
provisioning is not implemented. CONNECT proves possession of the registered key.
ServiceInstances.Provision awaits the ordinary native resource producer before
success (empty declarations and KV supported; other declarations fail explicitly).
Retry the same request after broker failure; retained allocations are never destroyed.

Auth.Resources.List/Get include all allocation states, including detached, with
digest resourceId, ownerKind (user/deployment), ownerId, and explicit state.
Declaration omission and deployment Remove detach and retain resource data;
Disable preserves resource bindings but revokes sessions and denies admission.
Enable reuses retained bindings without reapplying the contract or recreating storage;
there is no automatic resource deletion. Compatible re-add reuses retained data.
Explicit admin Resources.Remove permanently deletes only the selected detached
owned KV at expectedRevision after checking its physical ownership marker. Retry
the same manual request after broker failure; startup never resumes deletion.
Removal execution is exclusively claimed and incarnation-fenced. Recreating a
deleted logical resource uses a fresh allocation and physical bucket, so delayed
deletion cannot touch replacement data; compatible reattachment keeps the original.
KV history/TTL reductions that could lose retained data are rejected.

Auth Connections.Opened/Closed/Kicked publish generated AuthSecurityEvent values
through the admitted Auth provider. Event IDs and occurrence times survive durable
outbox retries; consumers should identify attachments by attachmentId and logical
authority by authorizationSessionId, not retired connection/session-key fields.
An expired delivery claim alone does not stop Auth: stale workers cannot
acknowledge or reschedule the intent, which remains recoverable by its next owner.

Trellis owns native contract compilation, generated APIs, authenticated
communication, connection lifecycle, and declared runtime resources. It does not
choose an application's configuration format, environment parser, database, ORM,
dependency injection, folder structure, UI framework, or testing policy.
Application-owned code can use other systems alongside Trellis.

The requirements below apply when using Trellis surfaces. For example, a Trellis
event's proof and subject are runtime-owned; that does not prohibit an
application from using a separate message system for unrelated work.

## Project And Generation

A minimal `trellis.toml` is:

```toml
[package]
name = "orders-trellis"
version = "1.0.0"

[sources]
orders = "contract.trellis"
```

Author APIs and participants in the `.trellis` files explicitly listed under
`[sources]`. An API defines models and public RPC, event, live, and operation
surfaces. A deployable participant identifies a service or device, the API it
implements, its selected dependencies, and its runtime resources. Apps and agents
instead author application request descriptors. A use body selects whole
capabilities: `required capability read;` is required and `capability export;`
is optional. Required wins when a capability is repeated; `use Api;` selects
nothing. Check capability availability before using an optional capability.
API authors declare positive `consent_revision` values; acceptance and
introduction counters are Auth-owned. Participant
identity, API identity, API release version, and surface transport version are
separate concepts.

Dependency commands:

- `trellis add` and `trellis rm` change dependency declarations.
- `trellis update` resolves dependencies and updates `trellis.lock`.
- `trellis install` reproduces locked dependencies and generated outputs.
- `trellis generate` compiles local IDL and generates packages using locally
  available dependencies. Use `--watch` for continuous offline generation.

Dependencies reference local or OCI native source packages. Remote locks pin
release and digests; credentials use the Docker credential configuration. If a
participant declares a durable `consumer`, add a direct `trellis` source package
dependency containing `trellis.events@v1` and choose its version in
`trellis.toml`. Run `trellis update` to lock it. Compilation fails if the
dependency or the Events API is missing; the platform does not choose a version
for the contract owner. Installation validates exact remote APIs in the global
content-addressed OCI cache, without a project-local installation tree. Direct
local dependencies contribute only requested APIs compiled from their own IDL,
without recursively resolving producer participants or manifests. Tooling
supplies validated API values to the compiler; it does not execute
source-language modules. Generation is offline; install missing remote
dependencies first.

Configure `[generate.rust].output` and/or `[generate.typescript].output`.

Each language gets one ordinary package at the source package version. APIs and
participants and app requests have separate `apis`, `participants`, and `apps`
module namespaces, not
independent packages or flattened root exports. TypeScript output contains
executable ESM `.js`, `.d.ts`, and `package.json`, with no consumer
transpilation step. Rust output is an ordinary path-dependency crate. Both
declare published Trellis runtime dependencies matching the CLI version.
Generation never edits the consumer's language manifests or chooses runtime
paths from repository ancestry. Use normal ecosystem overrides if developing
against a local runtime.

Each package contains generated APIs, participants, types, codecs, and runtime
descriptors. Published packages contain native source and frozen resolution
metadata, not canonical API/participant JSON. Generated descriptors are support
ABI, not a contract-as-code authoring surface.

Capability approvals are policy decisions over whole capabilities, not saved
exact-action grant snapshots. Administrative Auth actions also require the
applicable finite platform privilege; an ordinary capability never implies that
privilege. Own-authority/session maintenance is a fixed session right, not an
ordinary capability request. Resource commitments approve hard
semantics, while desired capacities are sizing hints and do not allocate larger
resources by themselves. Approval views distinguish requested commitments from
observed provider limits; runtime handles use the observed binding limits.
Trellis refuses to adopt or destroy a physical resource whose ownership marker
does not match. Removal detaches access without deleting new-version data;
compatible approved re-add reattaches the same resource identity. When running a
local Trellis environment, keep the platform database and NATS JetStream data
together. Trellis refuses to start the platform with a missing or different
JetStream identity after binding: restore the matching store or use fresh
platform and JetStream state and provision deployments again. Recreating
consumers and buckets alone does not recover job keys or stored objects.

State is one typed value without a key or TTL. KV is typed history and Store is
raw bytes. State/KV migration is direct and in-memory, with no write-on-read.
App State declarations request native State read/write/delete capabilities and
register JSON-schema UTF-8 bytes projected from native IDL before handle use.
Rust access is asynchronous: `let (state, registration) =
client.saved_resource("0", idempotency_key).await?;` (historical versions add
`&Migrations`). TypeScript retains `client.state.savedResource`; the first operation
registers at "0", or explicitly `await state.register("0")` to retain the revision.
Identical registration returns the current revision. Changes require explicit CAS
using the current registration revision; handle RegistrationConflict without blind
retry. Version schemas are immutable. Registration and value revisions are separate.
Typed `state.watch()` uses certified Live Watch for initial and subsequent snapshots,
with the same in-memory migrations as reads. Rust `observation.next().await` yields
`Option<Result<Option<StateValue<T>>, StateReadError>>`; TypeScript uses
`for await`. Inner None/undefined means unwritten or deleted. Close observations
explicitly for bounded cleanup; Rust drop and TypeScript iterator return also close.
`closed()` (Rust) / `closed` (TypeScript) reports the Live terminal outcome. No silent
reopen follows transport or authorization loss. The shared owner remains authoritative.
Generated Rust device State handles include SDK-owned native-IDL Watch support;
State-only devices need no built-in API package dependency. Completed device
activation rechecks reuse the retained challenge through authenticated enrollment,
not a new review; local completion never authorizes a disabled or removed device.
Operations are durable restartable at-least-once workflows. Consumers have local
per-process concurrency and Events-owned scoped DLQ/replay. Jobs remain private
durable queues. Cursor pagination ends only when `nextCursor` is absent and does
not generally promise a snapshot.

Commit IDL, `trellis.toml`, and `trellis.lock`, not generated implementations.
Run `trellis install` before compiling local SDK consumers; package generated code
when distributing a consumer. Trellis-owned Rust libraries build their built-in
bindings in Cargo `OUT_DIR` using published build dependencies, without a downstream
CLI requirement. Explicit generation targets select only the named outputs.
Compilation, renderer, and formatter failures preserve the last
successful generated outputs. Namespace collisions are errors, unrelated user
files are protected, and publication uses only short-lived staging and backups.

Selections must exactly match a name in the chosen API: `Get` and `Sites.Get`
are distinct. Invented prefixes are not qualifiers. Unsupported surface members
and incompatible constraints are compilation errors, not ignored options.
Numeric bounds accept finite JSON literals such as `-1` and `2.5`; string
lengths and list counts require unsigned integer literals. The IDL reference
documents each surface's members and each constraint's applicable types.

The generated names depend on declared action names and dependency aliases.
Check the generated participant, rather than inventing a method from a generic
example. TypeScript participants expose flat caller methods and generated
`handle...`, `publish...`, and `on...` methods where the selection allows them.
Rust participants expose typed methods through generated facades.

Rust schema-validation issue paths use JSON Pointer: an empty path addresses the
root, `/` addresses an empty-name property, and property names escape `~` as `~0`
and `/` as `~1`, including missing required fields.

## Connect And Authorize

Service/device bootstrap sends only provisioned identity and proof inputs.
Browser bind creates a user-login session and then performs context refresh.
These are different identity lifecycles, not interchangeable shortcuts. A device
companion is a native OAuth application request with independent user consent,
credential custody and connection. Accepted deployment registration creates
trellis.device.<deploymentId>.companion but grants no user authority. Provision
without identityPublicKey to issue a one-use provisioning secret bound to the
server-owned instance; /auth/device/enroll verifies durable and ephemeral key
possession. Devices.Reviews.Get/Decide require confirmation code and revision.
The companion separately completes normal OAuth Device Code consent and invokes
DeviceCompanions.Attach from that authenticated grant. Declare the Auth
deviceCompanionsManage capability in its request. A required wrapper refuses a
missing companion; an optional wrapper can connect without it. DeviceCompanions.Revoke
removes the association and revokes only its exact grant and refresh families,
leaving other grants, the user login and parent authority independent.
Removal permits the associated user or an administrator with current delegated
principals.manage. Removing the declaration rejects new and pending consent,
while existing independently consented grants retain ordinary refresh.

Browser sign-in uses OAuth authorization code with PKCE and DPoP. Public
credential-free discovery and issuer-chain metadata are readable before an
unknown application's HTTPS CIMD document is prepared. Client-bound token CORS
and cookie-authenticated Portal routes remain separate. Auth validates client
metadata retrieval, exact redirects, consent, and proof bindings.

Existing grants are reused only when shared issuance/policy semantics prove
compatibility without expanding approved authority; neither activity nor a
matching revision alone establishes eligibility. Compatible revision changes do
not force consent. Additional authority eligible for approval presents fresh
consent after authentication without a second password prompt. Stale consent
decisions are rejected and refreshed; policy denial is an authorization error,
while unavailable runtime/resource evidence remains bounded pending.

The SDK validates OAuth state, callback, PKCE and DPoP bindings before retaining
credentials. Browser custody is IndexedDB; Node custody is process-local memory
or an explicit application provider; the Rust CLI uses its native file store.
A valid login can authenticate new consent without another
password. Authorization denial is not a reason to create a login loop, and
consent cannot grant missing account entitlement.

Auth owns API-scoped capability grants, roles, OAuth consent, deployment
implementation rights, and resource allocations. Installing IDL grants nothing
by itself. Deployment Apply preserves verified unchanged resource evidence, not
pending or stale allocations. Service/device authority is deployment-owned and
separate from independently consented user companion authority. Read-only
capabilities do not grant write access.

`Auth.Capabilities.List` accepts optional `participantId`, `revision`, and
`sourceApi` filters. A participant plus revision selects an exact retained
snapshot; omitting revision selects that participant's current installation.
Revision requires a participant. With neither scope filter, discovery uses every
participant's current installation. Entries include `sourceApi` and `apiDigest`:
identical API definitions deduplicate, while differing definitions under the
same API ID remain distinct. Do not select an arbitrary definition by capability
identity alone. Console access editing scopes capability discovery and preset
expansion to the participant revision being edited, then saves exact
permissions.

For `trellis identity grants set`, the input file contains only
`installedRevision`, `grants`, `platformPrivileges`, and `expiresAt`; all four
fields are required. `installedRevision` accepts a JSON integer or decimal
string in `1..=9007199254740991`. `expiresAt` accepts `null`, or a JSON integer
or decimal string in `0..=9007199254740991`. The CLI normalizes these inputs for
the generated request. Omitting `--expected-revision` uses the current binding
revision, or zero for creation; an explicit zero is also valid. A stale revision
is rejected without changing the binding. `Auth.Users.Update` accepts optional
`username` to atomically rename an existing local credential and identity,
preserving the user ID and password; uniqueness conflicts roll back the
accompanying profile edits. Accounts without a local login establish one through
an account flow. `Auth.Users.PasswordReset.Create` targets `userId` and returns
a five-minute, one-use token for `/account/reset?token=...` on the OAuth origin.
Completion checks Origin/CSRF, credential CAS, and the requester's original active
logical session and current accepted `principals.manage`, then atomically changes
the password and revokes login/grant families. Bootstrap administrators use local
recovery instead. `Auth.UserIdentities.List`, `Auth.UserIdentities.Unlink`, and
`Auth.Users.IdentityLink.Create` target the current user. Linking returns a
five-minute portal URL, requires exact current-user continuity and fresh verified
upstream OIDC with nonce/PKCE, and rejects provider changes and identity collisions.
Creation replay keeps the original sealed response and never revives an action.
Last-sign-in-method and protected-administrator checks remain.
`Auth.Connections.List` accepts `principalId` to filter physical connections.

The server resolves assignment, installed artifacts, grants, resources, online
issuer, route JWT, inbox, and exact transports. Clients verify that response.
The libraries own proofs, context verification, proactive refresh, and transport
maintenance. Renewing unchanged transport authority promotes context and routing
credentials without replacing a healthy socket. Newly approved authority is
adopted automatically on a readied successor, while safe accepted work retains
its receiving connection. Retain the logical client, generated facades, and
still-bound resources across these changes; no manual transport refresh or
upgrade notification exists. Old sockets close after their retained work
releases them. Reduced or revoked authority, physical failure, and hard
authorization deadlines can interrupt affected work.

Fresh application IO cannot proceed when own revocation coverage is unavailable.
Bounded acquisitions wait within their budget; immediate acquisitions report
unavailability. Guarded registry maintenance restores continuous coverage on an
eligible admitted socket and wakes waiting calls. Successful make-before-break
watch migration preserves cached authority and existing leases; actual
revocation still fails closed. Jobs and durable event intake keep bounded
capacity across generations, with each delivery retaining its receiving
connection through disposition. Raw NATS connections are physical attachments,
not generation-aware application handles. Authorization contexts, route JWTs,
transport endpoints, grants, clock offset, and issuer keys are
process-memory-only. Browser IndexedDB version 3 persists only the initiating
session seed, nullable login metadata, pending signed intent/intent ID, and
generation tombstone, keyed by canonical origin plus stable participant ID.
Generation, public-key, intent, and login compare-and-swap fences prevent stale
tabs from overwriting or clearing newer state.

Trellis HTTP endpoints serve bootstrap, browser/account flows, recovery, and
browser assets. Connected Trellis control uses generated APIs over NATS. Use the
connected client's `logout()` for normal sign-out so local installation and
connection state are updated together. Self-revocation can close the transport
before the generated `Sessions.Logout` RPC reply arrives; `logout()` confirms
that the session is revoked through signed HTTP recovery when the reply is lost.
Unrelated authorization failures do not count as successful logout.

For multiple local managed-NATS servers, give each its own bundle and HTTP port,
and pass `--local-nats-ports=4223,8223,8081` with `trellis-server --dev` for a
second NATS client, monitor, and WebSocket port set. The default set is
4222/8222/8080; generated local configs use a 30-second owner lease renewed
every 5 seconds.

Message proofs bind the authority digest, exact API/action identity, API
generation/revision, actual subject, message identity, and exact payload bytes.
The signed authority supplies the originating session public key; message
headers do not establish another identity or carry permission lists.

Request verification checks caller grants against the caller's exact signed
catalog reference, independently of the provider's pinned implementation and
certificate. Compatible accepted revisions within one API generation need not
match; neither catalog grants additional rights to the other party.

Provider-owned event publication is authorized by the exact issuer-verified
event-publish action in the certificate bound to the signed native authority,
deployment, instance, implementation, API generation, and action introduction
revision. It does not require consumer capabilities. Delegated publication uses
whole-capability membership. Provider certificates cannot grant RPC caller or
event-consumption rights.

Historical event verification requires both the signed event timestamp and
trusted original JetStream publication metadata (`published` and
`stream_sequence`). Both timestamps must fall within the publisher authority's
validity window, and both must precede any ordinary session
revocation cutoff. A consumer's read time is not publication evidence; a
backdated signature cannot authenticate a new publication after expiry or
revocation. Current permission to read remains separate from past publisher
authenticity. Applications do not implement their own verifier or inspect
Trellis's internal authorization KV registry. Certified publication additionally
requires both timestamps within the provider certificate's validity window.
Ordinary certificate expiry or issuer retirement does not invalidate authentic
retained publications, including cold replay. Compromised issuers remain unusable.

## Choose A Surface

- RPC: a typed request and response, including declared business errors.
- Event: a published fact. Durable consumption uses participant-declared
  Consumer resources and can redeliver; handlers need an appropriate duplicate
  handling strategy for their side effects.
- Live: connection-scoped live data. Closing or aborting the subscription
  cancels provider work; it is not a durable event history.
- Operation: caller-visible asynchronous work with progress, terminal output,
  and optional cancellation, updates, or transfer.
- Job: service-private queued execution with retries and lifecycle state.

Parameterized events derive their concrete subjects from payload pointers; the
base subject includes the encoded qualified API identity, and listeners match
the generated wildcard pattern. Parameter values use unpadded base64url, and the
message proof binds the exact API, dotted event name, and parameter count. In
Rust, retain the returned listener guard: dropping or aborting it removes that
registration without stopping the other registrations in its group. Shared
pull-loop failures are reported by the service lifecycle, and unmatched messages
are not acknowledged as completed work. Durable names remain Trellis-owned.

Durable event success is acknowledged only after the handler succeeds. Retryable
failure uses the declared backoff; final exhaustion leaves delivery unacknowledged
so Events captures the broker max-deliveries advisory into that Consumer's DLQ.
Consumer ownership permits retained inspection and terminal replay reporting, not
administrative Replay/Dismiss. Manual replay
uses the same handler with a fresh delivery budget, does not rewind the original
Consumer, and confirms `resolved` before acknowledging success. Delivery and
application side effects remain at least once.

RPC cancellation stops the caller's wait, not work already accepted by the
service. TypeScript `RequestOpts.signal` reports `trellis.request.cancelled`
even after publication; deadline expiry reports `trellis.request.timeout`.
Neither undoes accepted work. Use Operation cancellation for business work.

Operations and jobs may expose typed live updates through an owned observation
session that is separate from the durable executor. A watcher reconciles the
current authoritative snapshot once its transport is ready, then delivers typed
transient updates and terminal state. Get and initial watcher snapshots expose
persisted state, not speculative handler state; a committed write may be visible
after its ACK is lost. Transient updates are ordered and never
silently dropped, while not-yet-delivered nonterminal snapshots may be
conflated. Updates are at-most-once, not persisted or replayed, and late
subscribers may miss them. Durable progress and terminal output are separate
from updates. Opening or closing a watcher does not start, cancel, or complete
the durable work. Operation get, watch, signal, and cancel remain authorized to
the creator principal plus participant, not a particular session or connection,
so reconnect can resume control. Completed, failed, and cancelled records are
immutable. Generated TypeScript service operation registrations expose the typed
local owner-fenced `.control(id)` and owner-routed `.reconcile(id)`.
Reconciliation serializes handler re-entry on the current owner with persisted
input, verified caller, and progress; it never steals a live lease. Cancellation
remains nonterminal during handler cleanup and owner lease renewal. `Cancelled`
is persisted only after the handler joins its owned side-effecting children; a
stalled cleanup has no forced terminal timeout. After owner loss, epoch fencing
does not prevent arbitrary external side effects from overlapping.
Before cancellation is observed, loss of the execution's receiving carrier or an
authoritative Operation state-read or watcher failure retires the local execution fence before handler code receives
the error and stops renewing that lease, allowing takeover after lease expiry
rather than persisting an invented business failure. Genuine cancellation cleanup
still renews its lease.
Cancellation-first admission requires both Invoke and Cancel authority before
durable reservation. Retry with the same caller-chosen invocation ID and input:
intent is atomic with fresh admission, merges into an exact existing invocation,
cannot be cleared by a normal replay, and does not change terminal records.
Reconciliation and recovery enter cleanup with the handler signal already
aborted; throwing, returning an error, or explicit deferral leaves cancellation
nonterminal. Native upload cancellation may have no transfer handle or staging;
check cancellation before accessing transfer resources. TypeScript exposes the
cancellation-first start option only for ordinary, non-transfer operations.

Keyed Jobs waiting for an active capacity slot maintain the current delivery and
do not consume a retry attempt before handler entry. `Jobs.Summary` computes all
matching totals, groups, and statistics independently of any `Jobs.Query` page.
Job deadlines are creation-relative. Omitted retry means five ordinary attempts
with delays of 5s, 30s, 2m, and 10m; explicit retry declares total attempts and
exactly attempts-minus-one positive ordered backoffs. Broker redelivery is
unlimited so execution owners can finish cleanup before Expired or Dead. Check
cancellation before business work: already-cancelled job handlers reconcile
earlier side effects, and cleanup errors preserve redelivery. Never-started
expiration confirms terminal publication before releasing recovered key slots,
without running handlers. Publication failure retains the reservation; terminal
redelivery reconciles any remaining slot before acknowledgement. Ordinary queues
use Block; stale-policy selection is not an authored option. Coordinator
fail-stale takeover fences the old attempt and atomically preserves its cleanup
obligation. The displaced job waits for capacity, recovers a fresh fence, and
reconciles with stale-attempt cancellation before settling Stale. Only confirmed
terminal settlement removes its obligation; the old token cannot mutate the
replacement owner's slot. Ignored stale completions are nonterminal diagnostics
and retain redelivery until cleanup settles. A never-started displaced
reservation settles Pending to Stale without handler execution.

Lifecycle publication in both SDKs awaits JetStream acknowledgement. Typed live
updates remain transient and do not require a durable stream. Execution state
and attempts follow accepted lifecycle transitions in broker stream-sequence
order. Created initializes but cannot reopen a job. Diagnostics, heartbeats,
logs, and progress cannot override settlement or attempts. A valid Retried opens
a new run under the same ID without deleting history. Work retains its original
lifecycle sequence through broker source metadata. Old-run deliveries are
acknowledged without touching newer-run coordination. Deferred work rereads
lifecycle state before acquisition. Live observations and Operation watchers are
authorized live sessions negotiated with bounded opening requests. The provider
signs its offer and frames; control responses bind the session ID, logical
command sequence, and command hash, and continued authority is rechecked from
retained context rather than by a network lookup per frame. A session has
protocol liveness and credit bounds, not a total age or message cap; closing
returns a receipt whose remote-cleanup state is complete, incomplete, or
unconfirmed, and reconnect is an explicit new open rather than a silent reopen.

Declare expected RPC/operation errors in IDL to obtain typed generated error
handling. Runtime validation and transport failures remain distinct from those
business errors. Application-local error handling is an application decision.

## Resources And Application Data

Connected services expose declared KV, Store, Consumer, and Job handles. Apps,
agents, and devices can declare State as one typed value without a key or TTL.
State/KV representation migrations run directly from accepted historical bytes
to current values in SDK memory and never write on read. State follows principal
and qualified participant identity across reconnects.

Bindings are runtime internals. Use generated resource handles instead of
constructing Trellis storage subjects or opening internal buckets. This does not
constrain the application's own database or external storage clients.
First-time provisioning can resume an interrupted allocation. Missing previously
materialized consumers, KV/object stores, Job keyed coordination, or Operation
storage fail closed; retries must not replace lost durable state with empty data.
Restore coherent durable state before resuming affected execution.
Identical deployment Apply retains only current ready resource evidence. Changed
or unmaterialized resources remain unavailable until reconciled; repeated Apply
does not promote stale evidence.
Runtime Jobs/Events resource evidence uses authenticated `Auth.ResourceBindings.Query`
with separate kind-scoped read capabilities and current binding digests. Split
roles never read another role's SQLite database. This is a runtime-internal
boundary; application services continue using generated resource handles.

Store and transfer APIs support streaming. Shared Store adapters pull finite,
byte-capped batches on demand and verify chunk order/count, size, and SHA-256
before successful EOF. Partial output is not a verified complete object.
Backend consumer expiry does not impose a reader idle limit: reads resume at the
exact next chunk while the pinned connection and stored chunks remain available.
Consumers are cleaned up before their generation lease is released; native
ObjectStore links are unsupported. Whole-buffer helpers collect the entire value
in memory, so bounded adapter buffering is not a whole-process memory guarantee.
Transfer v2 uses raw-byte one-way NATS DATA with bounded
frame/byte windows and cumulative consumed credit, not a request/reply per chunk.
Grants bind logical connection/session identities and exact session subjects,
never physical storage names, backend protocols, credentials, or presigned URLs.
Use generated upload Operations and high-level download helpers rather than
constructing grants. TypeScript consumers decode an RPC's untrusted `transfer`
field with `decodeTransferGrant(value).orThrow()`, check its direction, and use
`client.transfer(grant)`. The shared Rust/WASM decoder validates wire structure;
the transfer runtime separately verifies identity and authority.
In-flight transfers pin their admitting transport generation;
authority growth does not migrate them and physical disconnect interrupts them.

Transfers authenticate cancellation and completion and independently verify size
and SHA-256. Frames are bounded by negotiated peer payload limits, up to 1 MiB.
Credit follows downstream consumption, not durable persistence. Upload success
requires completed backend staging and durable Operation transfer commit before
the handler runs. A lost commit reply is not proof of rollback: staged bytes are
retained for durable reconciliation. Resume the Operation before retrying. Once
commit is underway, wire cancellation cannot promise an uncommitted outcome.
TypeScript's connection timeout bounds activation from transport acquisition
through the provider reply and separately bounds each cancellation exchange,
not the body lifetime. Cancellation timeout releases local ownership without
confirming remote cleanup. Watch transfer progress is monotonic and may be coalesced:
`chunkIndex`/`chunkBytes` identify the latest credited frame represented, not one
event per frame. Final persisted `transferredBytes` is exact. Interrupted uploads
restart from byte zero; partial replay/resumption is not supported.

Store and file metadata listing is key-sorted keyset pagination. The limit
defaults to 100 and must be at most 500. Cursors are opaque and bound to the
query, including its prefix; changing the query invalidates the cursor. Only
absent `nextCursor` means completion, and concurrent mutation means the pages
are not a snapshot.

Direct event publication does not atomically commit an application database
transaction. When that atomicity is needed, the SQL outbox integration can write
event/job intents in the same transaction. Trellis provides helper-table
migrations; the application owns its database, transaction adapter, and
migration execution. NATS KV outbox/inbox helpers are not atomic with unrelated
database writes. Rust SQL adapters require the opt-in `trellis-rs` features
`event-store-sqlite` or `event-store-postgres`; prepared events, memory stores,
and common store interfaces do not require a SQL driver. See the language guides
for the supported adapters.

Rust SDK HTTP connections and optional `telemetry-otlp` exporters preserve an
application-installed Rustls provider, otherwise use ring locally without
changing the process-wide provider, and verify certificates against platform
trust.

Outbox claims expire after 30 seconds and are recoverable; only the current
claim can complete. Publication can repeat after a crash, so this is not
exactly-once delivery. SQL inbox insertion returns true only to the caller that
inserted the marker, including under concurrency. Schema creation does not
upgrade old pre-release layouts; migrate retained databases explicitly.

## Optional Platform APIs

Declare these dependencies only when the application uses them:

- `Auth.Users.Resolve` supplies minimal display labels for known Trellis user
  IDs. It is not a general user directory or a restriction on application
  profiles.
- Jobs administration uses `Jobs.Query`, `Jobs.Metrics`, `Jobs.Inspect`, and
  `Jobs.Summary`, and `Jobs.Watch`. Summary is page-independent; Watch is an
  invalidation live, so reread the affected query and summary.
- Events offers event history, Consumer observability, and per-Consumer DLQ
  through its Query, Inspect, Metrics, Consumers, and Watch surfaces.

## Test And Troubleshoot

Choose application testing tools independently. For a test that needs real
Trellis transport, authority, or restart behavior, the npm package
`@oatscenter/trellis-testkit` provides `TrellisTestRuntime`. The published Rust
crate `trellis-testkit` provides the equivalent `TrellisTestRuntime` for Rust
test crates: it links the real production runtime in-process with no CLI/server
executable prerequisite, selects loopback ports automatically, and returns
normal SDK connection options for generated participants. Both harnesses run
real NATS child processes; the Rust bare builder defaults to the verified pinned
download, requiring network on first use. Its verified executable/archive cache
is shared (`TRELLIS_CACHE_DIR`, otherwise the platform cache); warmed-cache boots
work offline. Credentials, broker state, databases, PID files, and logs remain
sandbox-local. `TRELLIS_TEST_NATS_BIN` or
`NatsSource::Path` selects a prebuilt broker; `NatsSource::PathLookup` uses
PATH. Runtime/bootstrap Cargo dependencies are distribution-only implementation
crates, not service-author APIs. The TypeScript harness acquires its
exact-version production CLI/server from SHA-256-pinned release archives (currently Linux x86-64 only)
automatically: no installed Trellis or nsc required. Production commands
generate config and own managed NATS in a private sandbox with seeded admin.
`trellis: { source: { kind: "path", cli, server } }` selects an exact-version
prebuilt pair with no fallback. `restart()` preserves data/identity and restarts
the full host and broker. Stop first requests graceful host shutdown; on timeout
or host exit, isolated process-group cleanup reclaims remaining owned children
before sandbox removal. Startup requires `/readyz` metadata's `processId` to
match the spawned native host, not another runtime at the selected port.
`firstAdmin: "browser-flow"` opts into browser setup.
`TRELLIS_TEST_CACHE_DIR` reuses verified immutable binaries only. See
`/guides/testing-trellis-services`.

A missing generated method usually means the action was not selected or SDKs
need regeneration. Authorization failures require inspecting the installed
participant revision, current participant-scoped `GrantBinding`, required
resource evidence, principal/login state, and online issuer, not constructing a
raw subject or granting access in application code.

For runtime operation, see `/guides/starting-trellis`. For a complete service,
see `/guides/write-a-service`. Use `/api` for public language APIs and generated
source for project-specific names. Run the consumer repository's own checks
after generation; Trellis-repository xtask commands are not consumer commands.
Historical issuer keys are resolved through the existing issuer-signed metadata
exchange, authenticated by the active pinned issuer or its forward-verified
successor. Historical keys never advance live trust; compromised keys remain
unusable. A retired catalog signer does not invalidate an immutable catalog
referenced by current signed authority.
